title: When AI Agents Cross Chip Design Silos
gist: Chip design AI is shifting from large general LLMs toward specialized small language models and agents coordinated by orchestrating 'super agents', forcing EDA vendors (Synopsys, Cadence, Keysight, Siemens EDA) to re-architect tools around MCP/APIs and guardrails. Executives flag a $500M cost of error at 3nm/2nm, a talent gap that agents are backfilling, and a possible shift from software licenses to token-metered agents.

insights.claim: AI agents in chip design are becoming optimized for specific tasks, making it possible to use small language models instead of large language models for most jobs, since LLM agent swarms are overkill for most applications.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Shifts chip-design AI compute demand from frontier LLM inference toward cheaper, domain-tuned SLMs; favors vendors with proprietary domain data.
insights.quote: While LLMs can deploy swarms of agents for continuous reasoning and independent action, that’s overkill for most applications.
insights.locator: AI agents are becoming smarter, more capable

insights.claim: Movellus CEO Mo Faisal predicts only a couple of huge companies will own general LLMs while everyone else must specialize, arguing that using LLMs for workloads like weather prediction is inefficient.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Supports a barbell market structure: a few frontier-model owners plus many vertical AI specialists; value accrues to domain-specific model builders.
insights.quote: A couple of [huge] companies will take the LLMs, but everybody else has to specialize.
insights.locator: “The model is drawing a boundary,” said Mo Faisal

insights.claim: SiMa engineering leader Shriniwas Kulkarni says small language models are more efficient than quantized large models for specific RAG-based applications and can be trained on a company's own data for accuracy.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Edge/inference chip vendors like SiMa benefit if SLM + RAG becomes the default enterprise deployment pattern rather than quantized LLMs.
insights.locator: Small language models are well-suited for many specialized tasks

insights.claim: Using small language models and agents that are incapable of deconstructing sandboxes or scraping the entire internet is presented as a mitigation for rogue-agent risk, so silo barriers are crossed only when explicitly allowed.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Security/guardrail requirements add a second argument (beyond cost) for constrained domain models in IP-sensitive semiconductor workflows.
insights.locator: Those agents also need to be able to break through silos

insights.claim: Cadence's Matt Graham says aggregated 'super agents' are a new category of tools whose complexity and value could be as big or bigger than EDA tools themselves, with skills dynamically assembled into agents that customers script into their own flows.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Signals a new monetizable product layer for Cadence and peers on top of existing EDA licenses; watch for super-agent pricing and attach rates.
insights.quote: we think their complexity and the amount of value they can deliver is as big or bigger than EDA tools
insights.locator: “We’ve gone to the aggregation level with ‘super agents,’

insights.claim: Orchestrating specialized agents requires a different computing approach in which CPU-based orchestration may be as important as, or more important than, GPU-based multiply-accumulate operations.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Agentic workloads could lift demand for general-purpose CPU compute relative to pure GPU accelerators; relevant to CPU vendors and data-center mix assumptions.
insights.quote: CPU-based orchestration may be as important, if not more important, than GPU-based multiply-accumulate operations
insights.locator: The good and bad of specialization

insights.claim: Synopsys' Prith Banerjee says the company moved from per-tool question-and-answer agents to multi-agent workflows that mirror human teams resolving PPA trade-offs, such as clock gating lowering power but increasing area, which then needs an area expert.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Synopsys is positioning multi-agent coordination around cross-domain PPA optimization, a core pain point that justifies premium pricing.
insights.locator: “In our early work on agents,

insights.claim: ChipAgents CEO William Wang says the startup released a multi-agent solution in Q4 of the prior year for coordinated debugging, using multiple agents with parallel access to different contexts for large SoCs and functional/formal verification.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Startups like ChipAgents are shipping multi-agent verification products that compete with incumbent EDA agent offerings; potential M&A targets.
insights.locator: “You can have sub-agents do different things,

insights.claim: Baya Systems' Saurabh Gayen frames agent architecture as limited-scope agents plus a cross-cutting orchestrator built top-down and bottom-up, with human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and says no one has found a single perfect solution.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Agent architecture is still unsettled; be skeptical of any vendor claiming a definitive agentic EDA solution.
insights.quote: How you engineer those layers of agents is an art.
insights.locator: “We see people aligning to ideas about agents

insights.claim: Keysight EDA's Niels Faché says EDA vendors must redesign products built for human GUI use into modular capabilities exposed via Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and Python APIs so agents can stitch together code-based workflows.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: EDA incumbents face a re-platforming cycle; the vendor with the best agent-accessible APIs could gain share as flows become agent-driven.
insights.quote: So now we have to redesign our products.
insights.locator: “Typically, customers will work within a platform,

insights.claim: Guidance that used to live in EDA graphical user interfaces is being converted into example 'skills' handed to agents, paired with MCP servers that decompose a request such as designing a bandpass filter into executable steps.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Proprietary skill libraries and workflow examples become a competitive moat for EDA vendors.
insights.quote: What used to be guided in a graphical user interface is now in the form of example skills that you give to an agent
insights.locator: “If you want an agent to perform a certain task

insights.claim: Leading-edge chips, especially multi-die assemblies optimized for data centers, smartphones, or robotics, are often unique, which conflicts with the repeatability and predictability that agent actions and existing flows require.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Customization of multi-die designs limits reuse of agent learning across projects, slowing automation payback.
insights.locator: The integration problem

themes.theme: Data ontology and cost of error

insights.claim: Siemens EDA's Ankur Gupta puts the cost of a design or manufacturing mistake at $500 million at 3nm and 2nm, which is why AI engines must remain high-fidelity and deliver trusted outcomes.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Enormous error costs at leading nodes keep customers willing to pay for trusted, deterministic EDA, protecting incumbent pricing power against cheaper AI entrants.
insights.quote: The cost of a mistake is $500 million at 3nm and 2nm
insights.locator: There are business cases for this kind of behavior

insights.claim: Siemens EDA is building a data-ontology layer spanning chip, system, simulation, and PLM silos so LLMs and SLMs can operate on shared data and interact across domains, extending EDA into digital twins and real-world operation.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Siemens' PLM footprint could be a differentiator versus pure-play EDA rivals if cross-silo data layers become the basis for agentic design.
insights.locator: “There are still these silos,” said Ankur Gupta

insights.claim: Silvaco CEO Wally Rhines says fabs are not yet generating AI models, TCAD engineers are culturally conservative, and the opportunity is building real models from synthetic data calibrated against real fab data.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Process-modeling/TCAD is an under-penetrated AI opportunity; Silvaco is positioning for synthetic-to-real calibration agents.
insights.quote: The fabs aren’t generating these AI models yet
insights.locator: Models will follow, and agents will deploy them

insights.claim: Movellus' Mo Faisal notes a new job class in which top-1% domain experts are hired to talk to LLMs, reflecting that expert-trained synthetic data is a key input for AI models.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Expert-labeled training data is scarce and valuable; data-labeling and expert-network businesses benefit.
insights.locator: The data crush

insights.claim: Wally Rhines says no EDA vendor is yet pricing on tokens rather than traditional licenses, but customers are discussing it, and selling token-metered agents lets vendors capture value without ever seeing customers' proprietary physical data.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A shift from seat/term licenses to usage-based agent pricing would change EDA revenue visibility and margins; watch for first token-priced EDA offerings.
insights.quote: In some cases, you’d really rather sell an agent than software
insights.locator: “In some cases, you’d really rather sell an agent

insights.claim: Arteris' Michal Siwinski says the dot-com era drained talent from semiconductors and the experienced-engineer gap persists, so agentic AI is backfilling missing labor rather than acting as an accelerant.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Demand for agentic EDA is structurally supported by labor scarcity, not just productivity ambitions, making adoption less cyclical.
insights.quote: In this case, it’s not actually an accelerant. It’s backfilling.
insights.locator: But human engineers are also in short supply

insights.claim: Human engineers remain the glue that makes chip-design AI work, deciding how agents across design layers or manufacturing process stacks are optimized together, so AI enhances rather than replaces them.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Near-term chip-design AI is augmentation, limiting headcount-replacement narratives for EDA customers.
insights.quote: Human engineers effectively are the glue that makes AI work.
insights.locator: Human engineers effectively are the glue

themes.theme: Architecture churn and future chip companies

insights.claim: Mo Faisal compares today's AI shift to the early-2000s gigahertz-to-multicore transition, arguing architecture churns every 10–15 years, that the 'chip' is now the whole data center, and that the bottleneck will shift to data movement.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Favors interconnect, networking, and data-movement suppliers as the next AI scaling bottleneck.
insights.quote: Now the chip is the whole data center.
insights.locator: “You can draw parallels to the early 2000s,

insights.claim: ChipAgents' William Wang predicts multi-agent coordination will enable partly virtual chip companies staffed by virtual AI engineers.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Lower chip-design cost barriers could expand the number of custom-silicon designers, widening the EDA and foundry customer base.
insights.locator: “With multi-agent coordination, in the future

insights.claim: William Wang argues robotics has not taken off partly for lack of specialized chips (a robot takes 20 seconds to open a refrigerator versus one second for a human) and predicts robotics companies will build their own ASICs using AI chip-design platforms.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Physical-AI/robotics firms could become a new custom-ASIC customer segment for EDA, IP, and foundry providers.
insights.quote: in the future, robotic companies will build their own ASICs
insights.locator: If you look at physical AI and robotics

insights.claim: Arteris' Michal Siwinski says cross-domain multi-agent orchestration may get analog, verification, and formal engineers speaking a common language, and that the 'smart edge' is coming with reasons to create more unique software.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Edge AI device proliferation would drive more differentiated SoC designs and IP licensing.
